flagged.evidence: Step 2.2 says K∩p^{-1}(U_i) is compact because U_i is open. A compact set intersected with an open set need not be compact (for example, [0,1]∩(0,1)=(0,1)), so this does not license a finite subcover by sheets. Shrinking the finite evenly covered cover to relatively compact neighborhoods would supply the needed compact sets.

Step 10.1 treats K∩Ψ^{-1}(U_i) as compact because U_i is open. It need not be closed in K, so compactness does not give finitely many sheets covering it. A cover by smaller relatively compact evenly covered neighborhoods would justify the finiteness argument.

[F3] says “the group G is identified with the translation vectors Λ” and cites the definition of proper discontinuity. That definition only specifies the compact-set finiteness condition; it does not show that arbitrary plane biholomorphisms in G are translations. Step 2.1 establishes that later, so [F3] assumes an unproved conclusion and step 1.2 uses it before it is established.

Step 1.3 says connectedness of γ implies γ lies wholly in one of the two closures, although it has only shown γ⊂cl(A)∪cl(B). A connected set can be covered by two closed sets without lying in either one (a circle covered by two closed semicircles, for example). The local connectedness of the exterior half-disc at each boundary point must first show these traces are disjoint.

Step 6.2 claims every relatively compact coordinate disc in Ω has |G_{t_n}|≤C by step 5.1, but step 5.1 bounds G_t only on Y_t\(U_1∪U_2). Discs meeting U_1 or U_2 are not covered by that bound. The adjusted pole estimates of step 6.1 can bound compact subsets away from the poles, but they are needed before the diagonal extraction.
Step 1.2 says “γ∩\overline U=∅” and concludes γ⊂Y=X\overline U. But γ=∂U is part of the closed coordinate disc \overline U, so γ∩\overline U=γ and γ is disjoint from Y.

Step 2.1 says connectedness of γ implies γ⊂cl(A) or γ⊂cl(B), after only showing γ⊂cl(A)∪cl(B). Connectedness alone does not imply this for a cover by two closed sets; a local connected exterior half-disc is needed to show the two traces on γ are disjoint.

Step 1.1 infers from connectedness of γ and γ⊂cl(A)∪cl(B) that γ lies in one closure. Two closed sets can cover a connected circle without either containing it. The proof needs the local connectedness of the exterior half-disc to establish disjointness of the two traces.

Step 3.2 calls 0 a finite maximum of 1−ω when 1−ω≥0 and 1−ω(x)=0; this is a minimum. The stated maximum principle therefore does not establish strict positivity. It can be applied to ω, which has maximum 1 at x and is not constant because it is 0 on ∂Ω.

The Statement uses m_j for the integer logarithmic coefficient, but step 2.2 redefines m_j as the meridian class [λ_j*μ_j*bar(λ_j)] in π_1(W,x_0). Step 5.4 then writes φ_{x_0}(m_j)=…=−2πm_j, using the same symbol as both a fundamental-group element and an integer.

Step 6.2 derives that the component Z containing e_j is one-sheeted over D_j^×, then says local constancy over the connected base makes all of p^{-1}(D_j^×) connected and one-sheeted. Local constancy only makes the total fibre cardinal constant; it can exceed one, and knowing one component is one-sheeted does not exclude other components. Normality of N must be used to establish the needed property for every component.

Step 17.2 chooses z with U(z)>H(a)−ε, then chooses r and applies Harnack using |z−a|=r. The chosen z is not shown to lie on that circle, nor is r chosen after constraining z. Choose the small radius first and then choose z within it; the current order does not justify the displayed Harnack bound.

The Statement defines compact bordered Ω′ as a submanifold equal to the closure of its interior, so Ω′ includes its boundary. Step 1.1 nevertheless states a half-slice chart with φ(Ω′∩V)=φ(V)∩{y>0}; boundary points map to y=0 and are excluded from the right-hand side. Step 2.2 likewise treats R_i∩Ω′ as an open half-rectangle, which omits the boundary face used later.
